note: Key tenets per proceeding. Every quote is verified on its page by tools/verify-record.mjs.

groups.title: Rehearing of FERC's PJM Reliability Backstop Procurement order
groups.about: Seven parties ask FERC to reconsider its September order accepting PJM's backstop procurement. Asking for rehearing is the required step before a party can take an order to court.
groups.status: Seven requests, filed Oct 13 to Oct 29, 2026. FERC had not ruled on any as of Nov 9.

docs.filer: Joint Consumer Advocates (DE, DC, IL CUB, IL AG, MD, NJ)

tenets.tenet: FirstEnergy and NOVEC ask FERC to reject the procurement and replace it.

quotes.q: the Commission should reject PJM's RBP filing, proceed under the Section 206 proceeding it has instituted in Docket No. EL26-108-000, and establish settlement procedures.
requests that the Commission grant its request for rehearing and require PJM to adopt the voluntary stakeholder framework.
FERC should have rejected the RBP auction proposal and directed PJM to meet again with stakeholders to consider a model that would provide appropriate allocations of costs

tenets.tenet: Pay-as-bid without market power screens lets sellers bid the cap, not cost.

quotes.q: The Order accepts RBP without requiring reasonable market power screens or mitigation
unlike a uniform clearing price construct where sellers are expected to offer a marginal cost, sellers are more likely to offer the expected clearing price.
The RBP includes none of the BRA’s approved mitigation measures.
There is nothing in that structure that will prevent sellers from just bidding at the $555/MW-day offer cap regardless of the sellers’ actual marginal costs.

tenets.tenet: FERC abandoned its single-clearing-price precedent for capacity auctions without a reasoned explanation.

quotes.q: FERC also failed to provide a reasoned explanation for its departure from its long-held policy of requiring a single clearing price auction design for capacity markets.
A central premise of the design is that capacity sellers are expected to bid their own marginal costs.

tenets.tenet: The $555/MW-day cap is borrowed from the BRA with no evidence it fits.

quotes.q: The RBP Order fails to provide a reasoned explanation based on the record evidence for accepting an average-weighted $555/MW-day price cap.

The fact that the accepted auction design will pay each seller whose offer clears the auction its offer bid price for a period of up to 15 years only encourages rather than discourages offers above competitive levels.

tenets.tenet: 15-year terms could add $13 billion when five years would cure the shortfall.

quotes.q: The Order’s acceptance of RBP’s 15-year procurement terms could unjustly and unreasonably saddle captive ratepayers with some $13 billion in excessive and unnecessary RBP costs.
RBP’s acquisition of 15-year capacity commitments is unjust and unreasonable because it may increase

tenets.tenet: The levelized average-price framework lets sellers front-load payments into early delivery years.

quotes.q: FirstEnergy explained that the predictable consequence of this flexibility is that sellers will front-load their costs into the initial years of their contracts.

The Commission should grant rehearing and reject the levelized framework or, in the alternative, require that RBP offers be priced on a straight-line, fixed-value basis or subject to an annual price cap.

tenets.tenet: No locational requirement means RBP capacity may land where the load growth is not.

quotes.q: the RBP Order is arbitrary and capricious because it fails to engage arguments that RBP’s lack of locational constraints renders it unjust and unreasonable.
is likely to result in excessive capacity costs due to the non-deliverability of the resources to areas of need

tenets.tenet: Selection should favor firm, dispatchable resources, not just least cost.

quotes.q: The Commission should grant rehearing and require PJM to demonstrate that the RBP framework appropriately prioritizes firm and dependable capacity resources.
FirstEnergy further showed that PJM's selection process is designed to select the

tenets.tenet: Shortfall charges end at commercial operation, leaving customers unprotected for the rest of 15 years.

quotes.q: offers no explanation of what protects customers after commercial operation, when shortfall charges no longer apply.
FERC never addressed the IMM’s concerns that there is nothing to protect consumers from shortfall in capacity that could occur in years four through fifteen.
FERC did not explain why the shortage penalty, set at 20% of the price bid by the seller times the cleared capacity, was appropriate.

tenets.tenet: OCC: PJM's wording suggests consumers, not sellers, may end up paying the shortfall charges.

quotes.q: FERC also ignores that under PJM’s proposal, it is consumers who may pay the shortage penalties.

tenets.tenet: LSE collateral of $1.5 million per RBP MW is far above seller collateral.

quotes.q: Customers are asked to post collateral of $1.5 million per committed RBP MW to protect suppliers for up to fifteen years
the RBP Proposal is not just and reasonable because it imposes an unreasonable and excessive collateral obligation on RBP buyers

tenets.tenet: Demand response should need binding commitments, not just a plan for enabling equipment.

quotes.q: FirstEnergy therefore asked the Commission to require PJM to clarify that eligible demand response resources must be supported by binding contractual commitments.
A criterion that can be satisfied by a mere plan for the infrastructure necessary to deliver the offered load reduction does not serve that purpose

tenets.tenet: FERC should have finally rejected the TO Exit Amendment on cost-causation grounds.

quotes.q: The Order’s preliminary conclusion that the Exit Amendment may violate cost-causation principles should have been stated finally and definitively, instead of being left open for decision after a paper hearing.
the Commission has found it just and reasonable to impose generation capacity costs on LSEs located within an exiting TO’s zone, not on the TO as such.

tenets.tenet: PJM lacked section 205 authority to file the Exit Amendment over the TOs' CTOA rights.

quotes.q: PJM cannot avoid the CTOA’s amendment procedures by casting a change to the core terms of the CTOA as an amendment to the OATT, rather than to the CTOA.
Because PJM failed to fulfill any of these procedural prerequisites, PJM exceeded its authority in unilaterally submitting the Exit Amendment as a section 205 filing.

tenets.tenet: Clarification: an exiting TO should bear exit costs, and FERC has not presumed LSEs must pay.

quotes.q: Constellation seeks clarification that the Order neither established a presumption that LSEs in an exiting Transmission Owner’s zone must bear RBP exit charges nor predetermined the allocation of such charges.
An exiting Transmission Owner should bear its appropriate cost burden of generation and load investments made under the assumption that the Transmission Owner would remain in PJM.

tenets.tenet: The RBP should be the stakeholders' voluntary subscription model, with interruptible service as the alternative.

quotes.q: The PJM stakeholders proposed a voluntary framework for the RBP that recognized the contribution of load growth to the capacity shortfall without the issues attendant to PJM’s proposed RBP.
The Commission neglected to address NOVEC’s arguments that PJM should be required to adopt the voluntary, subscription-based model in lieu of the RBP Proposal.

tenets.tenet: Charging only LSEs serving large loads is undue discrimination, contrary to the IRAS order.

quotes.q: The RBP constitutes undue discrimination against LSEs that serve large loads.
The Commission cannot simultaneously maintain two opposing, contrary points of view and yet meet its obligation to engage in reasoned decision-making.

tenets.tenet: Price-taker RBP supply suppresses RPM prices and weakens entry signals for 15 years.

quotes.q: The resulting signal can reduce retention and entry incentives, accelerate resource exit, and defer new investment in the region.
The RBP suppresses the capacity price, which is the result whenever some generation must bid into the market as price-takers.
the Commission’s RMR precedent actually warrants rejection of the RBP due to the disproportionate, lasting impacts on the RPM’s ability to send accurate price signals.

tenets.tenet: RMR precedent cannot justify price-taker treatment of 6,831 MW for 15 years.

quotes.q: Characterizing the arrangements at that level of generality does not explain why their material differences are irrelevant, or why, in this instance, the price-taker requirement is just and reasonable.
The RBP is distinct as a matter of duration, exigency, and scale.

tenets.tenet: FERC ignored Constellation's isolation mechanism, which avoids double procurement without zero-price offers.

quotes.q: The mechanism therefore prevents duplicate procurement for the matched quantity by adjusting both supply and demand, while avoiding the one-sided price-forming effect of mandatory zero offers.

tenets.tenet: Energy-only plants like Eddystone should qualify as RBP Resources after obtaining new CIRs.

quotes.q: paragraph 51 rejected—without reasoned analysis—Constellation’s request to permit energy-only resources obtaining new capacity rights
The Order expressly recited Constellation’s request that Energy Resources obtaining new CIRs be eligible to provide Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW, but never decided it.

tenets.tenet: OCC: RBP costs should fall on the data centers that caused the shortfall, not other consumers.

quotes.q: FERC never addressed OCC’s main concern that the RBP auction model is inappropriate, unjust and unreasonable because it does not target procurement and allocation
OCC demonstrated that data center demand increased capacity costs to other PJM customers by approximately $23.1 billion across the 2025/2026, 2026/2027, 2027/2028 Base Residual Auctions.
direct PJM to work with stakeholders to develop an RBP auction design that will properly allocate related costs to the cost causers

tenets.tenet: NOVEC: the shortfall has other causes, so charging only large-load LSEs breaks cost causation.

quotes.q: Despite that fact, the RBP allocates all costs to LSEs serving large loads, a result inconsistent with the cost-causation principle.
NOVEC and other RBP Buyers would be subsidizing the rest of the capacity market, a result that is not consistent with the cost-causation principle.

tenets.tenet: AMP: PJM's allocation holds, because Table B9b counts the large loads FERC feared missed.

quotes.q: Because the Load Adjustments in Table B9b are intended to count new large load quantities, including those that might have otherwise been embedded in the initial PJM load forecast data, use of Table B9b addresses the Commission’s principal concern
The Commission should clarify that it has not made a final decision regarding the justness and reasonableness of PJM’s as-filed RBP cost allocation approach

tenets.tenet: AMP: FERC's suggested load-difference method must not charge zones without large-load growth.

quotes.q: implementing its potential modification to RBP cost allocation would likely violate cost causation principles, as it could result in the allocation of RBP costs to zone/areas that have not experienced load growth attributable to data centers or other large loads.

tenets.tenet: Constellation agrees Load Adjustments may miss large loads and wants current, validated forecasts used.

quotes.q: The Order correctly found that reliance on PJM’s Load Adjustment process may fail to capture actual or forecast large-load growth
Any replacement methodology must use current, project-specific, PJM-validated and auditable information; identify and eliminate double counting associated with duplicate or alternative-site requests

tenets.tenet: Clarification: the cost-allocation paper hearing stays open to all methods, including NOVEC's causation arguments.

quotes.q: NOVEC respectfully requests that the Commission dispel any ambiguity as to the scope of the paper hearing and clarify that the Commission has set all issues concerning cost allocation for further procedures

tenets.tenet: Clarification: the collateral paper hearing should cover credit rate size, overlapping collateral and release standards.

quotes.q: Constellation requests clarification that the paper-hearing inquiry into “appropriate collateral requirements for RBP buyers” encompasses: (1) the size and methodology of the RBP Credit Rate;

tenets.tenet: TOs and FirstEnergy seek rehearing mainly to preserve issues while PJM prepares a replacement filing.

quotes.q: The Indicated PJM Transmission Owners submit this rehearing request out of an abundance of caution to preserve their rights in this fast-moving and dynamic proceeding.
rehearing is still warranted to ensure these issues are preserved and appropriately decided in the context of any new filing made by PJM.

groups.title: MISO Large Load Addition Resource Study (LARS)
groups.about: MISO, the grid operator for 15 states in the Midwest and South, wants to study a new load of 200 MW or more together with the power plant built to serve it, in about 120 days and outside its multi-year generator queue.
groups.status: Comments and protests were due Oct 23, 2026. MISO asked for a Dec 2, 2026 effective date; FERC had not acted as of Nov 9.

docs.filer: Sierra Club, NRDC and other clean energy and community groups

tenets.tenet: LARS studies a 200 MW-plus load and its paired generation together in about 120 days.

quotes.q: LARS will provide a path for the interconnection of both large loads and supporting generation pairs in a parallel 120-day study process.
LARS offers a coordinated, 120-day parallel study of eligible large loads and their paired generation resources.
LARS provides for a 120-day parallel study of eligible large loads and their paired generation resources.

tenets.tenet: Supporters say studying load and generation together removes duplicative upgrades and lowers costs.

quotes.q: The goal of LARS is not necessarily to find the lowest cost solution for either the load or generation but to identify the solution that best fits both
This integrated approach will enable MISO to identify optimized transmission solutions, eliminate duplicative or unnecessarily expensive upgrades, and help deliver lower-cost outcomes for customers.
By studying load and its paired generation together, MISO can identify combined transmission solutions, avoid duplicative and costly upgrades, and produce an outcome in approximately 120 days.

By allowing large loads and associated generation resources to be studied together, the proposal recognizes that jointly planned and electrically proximate resources may produce materially different system impacts

tenets.tenet: Utilities say MISO's generator queue takes years, so paired generation needs a faster lane.

quotes.q: MISO's DPP cycles have taken four years or longer to reach completion, leaving load-serving entities without a timely path to interconnect associated generation
LARS meets the urgent need for an accelerated evaluation process that accounts for both load and generation

tenets.tenet: MISO says LARS answers the Show Cause Order and leaves the generator queue untouched.

quotes.q: LARS provides a mechanism for MISO to study a large load and the generation that will serve it at the same time
As a result of the way MISO's study models are structured, LARS projects will not impact existing projects in the DPP process.
The LARS filing also preserves an open and non-discriminatory framework by permitting the interconnection customer responsible for the generation component to be any eligible entity.

tenets.tenet: Entry limits cap LARS at ten pairs per study period and three periods a year.

quotes.q: There will be three LARS study periods each year and each study period will be completed in approximately 120 days
MISO will accept ten LARS Applications per study period and the LARS Applications will be assigned to study periods in order of submission.
can administratively support the new process, as only ten generation/load pairs per study period will be evaluated, with three periods per year.

tenets.tenet: Applicants must post $250,000, show site control, and sign a five-year pairing contract.

quotes.q: A non-refundable fee of $250,000 must accompany the LARS Application and be paid by the LARS Associated Transmission Customer.
The agreement must be legally binding and must state a minimum term of five years
limiting the amount of requested Interconnection Service to no more than 150% of the peak demand of the LARS Associated Load, and demonstration of 100% site control

tenets.tenet: The load must be 200 MW or more at one point of withdrawal, unaggregated.

quotes.q: must be a large load of at least 200 MW
While MISO is allowing aggregation for LARS Generating Facilities, MISO is not allowing aggregated load to participate in LARS.

tenets.tenet: Generation must connect in the load's Local Resource Zone, which can span several states.

quotes.q: Another important condition of the LARS process is the requirement that the load and generation pair be located in the same Local Resource Zone

Neither MISO Witness Drake nor the Transmittal Letter explain how the LARS proposal mitigates the electrical impact of LARS Associated Load and generation facilities being spaced potentially hundreds of miles apart

tenets.tenet: The pair must stay together 15 years; if the load leaves, the generator gets a year.

quotes.q: MISO will provide the Generating Facility up to one year after the LARS Associated Load withdraws to continue to operate under the LLGIA

this requirement ensures that the LARS study process accurately reflects the expected impacts of the Generating Facility and LARS Associated Load on the Transmission System for a significant period of time.

tenets.tenet: Upgrades for violations seen in the load study, or in both studies, go to zonal load.

quotes.q: Then any common violations that show up in the generation and load studies are assigned to BRP and Other project types. Only the violations but for the generator are assigned GIP project types.

Unlike the violations observed only in the generation study, the LARS Process assigns the cost of network upgrades to address violations observed in the transmission studies and observed in both the transmission study and the generation study to Baseline Reliability

tenets.tenet: MISO says double-allocated headroom gets fixed later through MTEP projects, paid by zonal load.

quotes.q: In the event that overallocation does occur, any constraints that are identified as needing mitigation in the MTEP process will be formalized in a future MTEP project.
The cost of the MTEP project will be allocated based on existing Tariff rules, which is likely to be the load within the transmission pricing zone where the transmission upgrade is required.

tenets.tenet: MISO will file its cost-shifting agreement by November 16, 2026; LARS need not wait.

quotes.q: all of which will be submitted to the Commission in a FPA section 205 filing by November 16, 2026.
LARS can be implemented based on the Tariff revisions filed herein and need not await these future filings.

tenets.tenet: LARS puts upgrade costs of load-caused violations on zonal ratepayers instead of the pair.

quotes.q: Under current rules, the costs of those project types are recovered from all network customers in a Transmission Pricing Zone.
LARS, therefore, takes a category of costs usually assigned to generators and assigns them to existing load.
The LARS proposal does not adequately assign costs to the cost causers, and MISO has not yet fully developed a cost allocation proposal for LARS load and

tenets.tenet: FERC cannot find LARS just and reasonable without MISO's unfiled cost-shifting agreement.

quotes.q: the Commission cannot determine that LARS is just and reasonable because the record lacks such a key piece of the puzzle.
A process that assigns upgrade costs to zonal load now, on the strength of an agreement whose terms are not before the Commission, has not been shown to be just and reasonable.
The Commission should require MISO to address cost-shifting in all of its Section 205 filings and in all of its direct responses to the Section 206 Show Cause Order.

tenets.tenet: Google: reject LARS with guidance, or accept and suspend it until the cost agreement arrives.

quotes.q: the Commission should either reject LARS with guidance indicating that it needs to be filed concurrently with procedures to prevent cross-subsidization or, in the alternative, accept and suspend the proposal
Google supports the intent and conceptual direction of LARS.

tenets.tenet: LARS and the queue use different assumptions, so both can claim the same headroom.

quotes.q: each process is based on an incomplete snapshot of the transmission system and how it will operate in practice, which increases the likelihood that the LARS and DPP processes will produce incompatible results.
LARS projects will therefore be studied as if the only other generation on the system is generation that already holds a GIA.
These differing approaches risk MISO allocating transmission headroom twice.
Under the proposal, LARS and DPP requests will be studied separately and using different assumptions.

tenets.tenet: Queued generators say overallocation raises their upgrade costs and curtails their output.

quotes.q: resulting in more constraints and higher Network Upgrade costs for DPP projects when they are finally studied against a system that LARS projects have already used.
Failing to coordinate DPP and LARS shifts costs onto DPP customers.
The filing does not adequately explain how MISO will coordinate transmission-capability assumptions across parallel interconnection processes.

tenets.tenet: Google would model advanced-stage queue projects in LARS so large loads absorb study error.

quotes.q: LARS could be modified to use more conservative assumptions

tenets.tenet: Utility gatekeeping of LARS applications is undue discrimination against independent generators.

quotes.q: MISO proposes to effectively grant the Transmission Customer, which has an incentive to discriminate against competitive generation, the ability to discriminate against competitive generation.
LARS is unduly discriminatory because it makes the LSE the gatekeeper of a Commission-jurisdictional generator interconnection process
making load-serving entities ("LSEs") the gatekeepers of the LARS process
In other words, the LSE is the gatekeeper for participation in LARS, because without it

tenets.tenet: MISO says only the transmission customer can buy transmission service, so it must file.

quotes.q: Because only the Transmission Customer can procure Transmission Service under established Tariff processes, LARS requires the LARS Associated Transmission Customer to be the party that initiates the LARS Application
This does not supersede the role of the LARS Associated Transmission Customer to determine whether to submit a LARS Application

tenets.tenet: SEIA and United: reject LARS and let any qualified party file; or require nondiscriminatory handling.

quotes.q: reject the LARS proposal, on the grounds that the proposal is unduly discriminatory, and provide guidance to MISO to refile the proposal with a mechanism that would allow any qualified market participant

the Commission should clarify that once an applicant meets all applicable LARS eligibility, readiness, financial security, and application requirements, the Commission expects the LARS Associated Transmission Customer to apply the same submission standards

tenets.tenet: Google wants independent generators to have direct access, with FERC resolving disputes with the utility.

quotes.q: protections providing that all forms of generation, including independent generation, have nondiscriminatory, direct access to the expedited generation interconnection study process under LARS.

tenets.tenet: LARS is a permanent, uncapped fast lane untethered to any identified resource adequacy need.

quotes.q: It is permanent and uncapped. It is untethered to any identified resource adequacy need.
LARS is not time-limited, as MISO's most recent queue-jumping proposal ERAS was.
The Joint Protestors are concerned that LARS, similar to ERAS, will enable queue jumping.

tenets.tenet: Unlike ERAS, LARS has no cap, sunset, independent-producer carve-out, or regulator check.

quotes.q: LARS contains no scoring criteria, no carve-outs, no regulatory verification, no cap, and no sunset.

tenets.tenet: Same-LRZ pairing is not the two-substation test the Show Cause Order described.

quotes.q: Instead, LARS generators and load are merely required to be in the same general Local Resource Zone.
The Joint Protestors respectfully urge the Commission to require MISO to establish a reasonable distance of "electrically proximate"
LARS does the opposite: it grants permanent NRIS through a parallel process

tenets.tenet: LARS generators get full capacity-market access years before other queue generators.

quotes.q: MISO's proposal is unduly discriminatory because it grants generators associated with qualifying large loads an accelerated pathway to obtain access to MISO's Planning Resource Auction market

tenets.tenet: If the paired load leaves, the generator faces a one-year bridge into a backlogged queue.

quotes.q: The proposed transition mechanism is woefully inadequate to address this stranded asset risk.

tenets.tenet: After 15 years the generator keeps full NRIS even if its load is gone.

quotes.q: After fifteen years, the generator keeps full NRIS of up to 150 percent of the departed load's peak demand with no further study and no cost at all.

tenets.tenet: Bloom: the 200 MW floor has no impact data behind it; lower it to 50 MW.

quotes.q: LARS should therefore apply to loads of 50 MW or more that connect to the Transmission System.
MISO presents no EPR results or other grid impact study for 200 MW, and none for loads below it.

tenets.tenet: Bloom: accept LARS by December 2, then order a 60-day compliance filing on the threshold.

quotes.q: Bloom does not ask the Commission to delay LARS.
Bloom supports LARS and urges the Commission to accept it by MISO's requested December 2, 2026 effective date.

tenets.tenet: Consumer advocates object to exempting about 30 GW of existing large load from reliability rules.

quotes.q: In total, MISO is proposing to fully or partially exempt approximately 30 gigawatts of existing load from the Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements.

tenets.tenet: Clean energy groups say LARS adds a fifth path onto the grid and breaks planning.

quotes.q: LARS would be at least the fifth separate path onto the MISO transmission system
By excluding the DPP, LARS does the opposite of NERC's procedures.
MISO has now twice prioritized separate, one-off expedited processes that not all market participants can feasibly access on a comparable, not unduly discriminatory basis

tenets.tenet: ACP and SREA: MISO has not met the independent entity variation standard.

quotes.q: MISO cannot satisfy the independent entity variation standard, and LARS does not accomplish the purposes of Order No. 2003

tenets.tenet: Protesters ask FERC to reject LARS outright; Clean Energy Advocates offer a deficiency letter instead.

quotes.q: the Commission should reject all portions of MISO's LARS proposal and direct MISO to engage with stakeholders to advance a different proposal.
the Clean Energy Trades respectfully request that the Commission reject MISO's LARS proposal.

tenets.tenet: If FERC accepts LARS, ACP wants the same-LRZ test applied at the point of interconnection.

quotes.q: the relevant location is the applicable POI to the MISO Transmission System rather than the physical location of the Generating Facility

tenets.tenet: Supporters want FERC to accept LARS as filed, citing its entry limits and fuel neutrality.

quotes.q: stringent eligibility requirements to deter speculative interconnection requests and minimize disruption to the DPP

These requirements provide reasonable assurance that participating projects represent durable load-generation relationships and help mitigate potential impacts to the transmission system and other customers.
MISO's proposal is transparent, competitive, fuel agnostic, and it does not adversely affect DPP participants.
Strong readiness requirements are therefore an appropriate safeguard against speculative projects consuming scarce study resources
agrees with the comments made by the Mississippi Public Service Commission and the Louisiana Public Service Commission.

groups.title: PJM Reliability Backstop Procurement
groups.about: PJM, the grid operator for 13 states and D.C., proposed a backstop purchase of new power plants to cover a projected supply shortfall as large loads grow. FERC accepted it in September and sent three cost questions to a written hearing.
groups.status: Accepted and suspended Sep 29, 2026, with cost allocation, transmission owner exit rules and LSE collateral set for paper hearing. PJM refiled amendments Oct 29 in ER27-330-000; comments are due Nov 30.

tenets.tenet: FERC accepts the backstop, suspends it to February 28, 2027, and sets a paper hearing.

quotes.q: we accept the proposed RBP for filing, suspend it for five months, effective February 28, 2027, subject to refund, and establish a paper hearing

tenets.tenet: Only cost allocation, TO exit rules and LSE collateral go to hearing; the rest stands.

quotes.q: Aside from the three issues discussed directly below, we find that the other aspects of PJM’s RBP proposal are just and reasonable

tenets.tenet: The backstop buys 6,831 MW, the 2028/29 auction shortfall, less offsets and opt-outs.

quotes.q: the RBP aims to procure capacity equal to the 6,831 MW shortfall in the 2028/2029 BRA (Initial RBP Target)

tenets.tenet: Winning resources get fixed terms of up to 15 years, from 2028/29 through 2042/43.

quotes.q: for a fixed term of up to 15 years, starting with the 2028/2029 delivery year at the earliest and ending no later than the 2042/2043 delivery year
we disagree with JCA that PJM unreasonably requires commitment terms ending no earlier than 2042/2043

tenets.tenet: FERC approves the $555/MW-day price cap and the pay-as-bid selection process.

quotes.q: we find that PJM has shown that its proposed $555/MW-day maximum willingness to pay and process for selecting RBP Resources in the RBP auction are just and reasonable
We agree with PJM that the proposed pay-as-bid structure for the RBP auction is reasonable.

tenets.tenet: FERC accepts a 120% UCAP quantity cap, 20% shortfall charge, for up to three years.

quotes.q: We agree with PJM that the proposed cap represents a reasonable balance between providing sellers with flexibility and managing UCAP risk for load.
RBP shortfall charges are equal to the product of the RBP Resource’s committed RBP UCAP MW shortfall and 20% of the RBP price.

tenets.tenet: A zonal growth snapshot may be fine; measuring growth with Load Adjustments may not be.

quotes.q: we agree with concerns in the record that relying on Load Adjustments to measure load growth may be inconsistent or not reasonably capture forecasted load growth or actual large load growth
it appears some large loads may never have been accounted for as Load Adjustments because PJM accounted for them when calculating the initial load forecast

tenets.tenet: FERC floats 2026/27 actual load against the latest 2028/29 forecast as the allocation basis.

quotes.q: PJM could base the RBP allocation on the difference between the actual load for 2026/2027 delivery year in each Electric Distributor zone/area with the most recent 2028/2029 delivery year load forecast

tenets.tenet: The co-op and municipal opt-out may discriminate, since their large loads are similarly situated.

quotes.q: We find that PJM’s proposed opt-out for qualifying cooperatives and municipal utilities may be unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.
Because cooperatives and municipal utilities serve large loads that are similarly situated to large loads served by other LSEs

tenets.tenet: FERC keeps FRR entities out of the backstop because they never contributed to the gap.

quotes.q: we find that FRR Entities have not contributed towards the resource adequacy gap that the RBP will address

tenets.tenet: FERC leaves charging data centers at retail to the states and the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.

quotes.q: states determine how Commission-approved rates are collected among the relevant retail consumers along with the rates for state-jurisdictional matters
Our partners in the states are more than capable of ensuring that these promises reach fruition.

tenets.tenet: Exit fees on departing Transmission Owners may be unjust; LSEs are the buyers and beneficiaries.

quotes.q: we find that PJM’s proposed exit provisions may be unjust and unreasonable because they would assess RBP Charges to exiting Transmission Owners, rather than the LSEs in the relevant Transmission Owner’s zone

tenets.tenet: The $1.5 million per MW buyer collateral rate lacks quantitative support and may be unjust.

quotes.q: PJM does not support its 50% estimate with any quantitative measures, including an expected probability of default
we find PJM’s proposed collateral requirements for RBP Sellers just and reasonable

tenets.tenet: The existing reliability backstop auction tariff may itself be unjust, so FERC opens EL26-108.

quotes.q: We therefore conclude on a preliminary basis that the existing Reliability Backstop Auction Tariff provisions may be unjust and unreasonable.

tenets.tenet: FERC invites a 205 refiling within 30 days and says it would expect to grant abeyance.

quotes.q: we anticipate that the Commission would grant a motion to hold that briefing in this proceeding in abeyance if PJM submitted a new section 205 filing within 30 days from the date of this order
We anticipate that, following the paper hearing, the Commission may need to direct significant modifications to certain aspects of PJM’s proposal

tenets.tenet: The 2027/28 auction cleared at the $333.44 cap, a third straight historically high result.

quotes.q: The 2027/2028 BRA, which cleared at the temporary price cap of $333.44/MW-day, was the third BRA in a row to clear at historically high prices.

tenets.tenet: DOE backs the order and wants PJM to refile by October 29 to protect ratepayers.

quotes.q: DOE urges PJM to accept the accelerated option proposed by the Commission and to swiftly submit a revised tariff pursuant to FPA section 205 on or before October 29, 2026.

PJM should implement the cost allocation and other reforms identified by the Commission to ensure that the costs of serving new data centers or other large electric energy loads are not unfairly shifted to PJM’s existing ratepayers.

tenets.tenet: DOE says PJM's two-year lookback lets large loads ride free on the shortfall.

quotes.q: PJM’s cost allocation methodology (looking back only two years) does not appear to sufficiently allocate the costs of new capacity to serve all large loads that have caused the current resource adequacy shortfall
PJM should ensure that any cost allocation methodology properly allocates costs and does not result in free ridership.

tenets.tenet: DOE wants mandatory project-level large load identification and a clear build, bring or buy path.

quotes.q: DOE agrees with the Commission’s call for improved large load identification and transparency to support a just and reasonable cost allocation.

groups.title: PJM Large Load definition, Registry and Interim Resource Adequacy Service
groups.about: PJM asked FERC to define a Large Load, keep a registry of them, and create a service that would curtail such loads first in a supply emergency. FERC kept the definition and the registry and rejected the rest.
groups.status: Issued Oct 9, 2026. PJM's compliance filing and any rehearing requests were due Nov 9; neither was on eLibrary that morning.

tenets.tenet: FERC accepts a 50 MW cumulative-peak threshold as the Large Load definition.

quotes.q: establishing the threshold to qualify as a Large Load at a cumulative peak of 50 MW strikes a just and reasonable balance between capturing the larger loads into which PJM needs visibility to ensure the reliability of its system

tenets.tenet: FERC accepts the Large Load Registry and severs it from the rest of the filing.

quotes.q: We find that PJM’s proposed Large Load Registry is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential because it will require LSEs to provide information about the Large Loads that they serve to PJM

the only elements of its proposal that are severable are the proposed definition of Large Load and the proposed Large Load Registry, which can be implemented independent of the IRAS and BYONC frameworks.

tenets.tenet: FERC rejects IRAS because it appears to intrude on retail rate regulation.

quotes.q: certain aspects of PJM’s proposal appear to present an impermissible intrusion on retail rate regulation and are not subject to the Commission’s authority pursuant to section 205

tenets.tenet: The tariff text, unlike PJM's transmittal, puts curtailment duties directly on retail large loads.

quotes.q: the plain language of the Tariff, as proposed, appears to place obligations directly on the Eligible New Large Loads and requires Electric Distributors to curtail the Eligible New Large Loads.

tenets.tenet: FERC finds IRAS compensation sets a retail rate, which only states may do.

quotes.q: the proposed Tariff appears to be setting a retail rate because it establishes a compensation rate for IRAS payable to the Eligible New Large Load.

tenets.tenet: FERC says PJM did not justify treating utilities differently based on retail customer traits.

quotes.q: PJM’s proposal imposes capacity procurement and curtailment obligations on Electric Distributors and LSEs taking NITS to serve certain loads based on retail customer characteristics
PJM’s generic references to these retail customer characteristics without more detail are insufficient evidence

tenets.tenet: FERC rejects the BYONC accreditation lock-in for lack of record support.

quotes.q: PJM has not sufficiently justified its proposal to lock in the accreditation of BYONC resources over the lifetime of the BYONC arrangement

the risk that a BYONC resource’s locked-in accreditation value be higher than the capacity that it can actually provide has the potential to create a new resource adequacy risk for the entire PJM Region

tenets.tenet: FERC rejects excluding new large loads from the VRR curve as inseparable from IRAS.

quotes.q: the proposed rules for BYONC arrangements and the exclusion of Eligible New Large Loads from the VRR curve, are not simply complementary, but instead are inextricably linked.

tenets.tenet: FERC grants that PJM faces a capacity shortfall but says the proposal falls short.

quotes.q: we recognize the imminent capacity shortfall in PJM, we find that two key aspects of PJM’s proposal—IRAS and BYONC—are either outside of the Commission’s authority or have not been sufficiently demonstrated
beginning in the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, it will be short of sufficient capacity to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement, particularly due to data center load growth

tenets.tenet: FERC warns IRAS would shed firm load at EEA1, earlier than the reliability standard allows.

quotes.q: PJM’s proposal would shed firm load on an involuntary basis.

tenets.tenet: FERC doubts load excluded from the VRR curve should pay capacity charges.

quotes.q: Eligible Customers taking non-firm transmission service on behalf of co-located load should not be charged for capacity because PJM does not procure capacity on their behalf.

tenets.tenet: FERC keeps manufacturers in the Large Load definition, not just data centers.

quotes.q: the one-mile radius paired with the single electrical site requirement is necessary to ensure that loads that are physically located together and affiliated are considered as a single facility

tenets.tenet: FERC says a cutoff just below 50 MW is not unjust merely because it excludes loads.

quotes.q: any cutoff criterion would inevitably exclude loads sized just below the threshold, and that alone does not render the definition unjust or unreasonable.

quotes.q: we also sever and reject the definition of New Large Load without prejudice.

groups.title: PJM co-location compliance
groups.about: Co-location means a large load, usually a data center, built at a power plant and served partly by it. FERC set rules for it in PJM; these filings carry them out.
groups.status: PJM filed partial compliance Aug 17, 2026 and answered three limited protests Oct 14. The rest of its compliance is due Nov 16.

tenets.tenet: FERC gives PJM and its owners 90 more days, to November 16, on co-location.

quotes.q: The deadline for PJM to comply with certain directives of the Co-Located Load Order, and the deadline for the PJM transmission owners to comply with the directives of the Co-Located Load Order, is extended to and including November 16, 2026.

tenets.tenet: The extension lines co-location compliance up with PJM's large-load section 205 filing.

quotes.q: to allow PJM to develop the remaining aspects of its compliance filing to comply with the Co-Located Load Order in conjunction with a Federal Power Act section 205 filing being developed in response to the Large Load Show Cause Order
